data.heading: Letter names
data.text: A is called /a/, B is /be/, C is /se/. A letter name is what you say when spelling; it is not a promise that the letter always sounds the same in words.

data.heading: Two jobs for C
data.text: The name C is /se/. In café, c begins with /k/; in ici, c sounds /s/. The next letter helps determine the sound.

data.heading: Spell in chunks

data.heading: Check your ear
data.text: G /ʒe/ and J /ʒi/ share /ʒ/ but have different vowels. Today learn G; J follows tomorrow.

data.heading: A and I
data.text: In ami /ami/, a is open /a/ and i is a high front /i/. Each written vowel contributes a clear beat.

data.heading: O and OU
data.text: The o of mot is /o/ and final t is silent. The two letters ou represent one vowel /u/ in vous.

data.heading: U versus OU
data.text: U in tu is /y/; ou in tout is /u/. Change the lip and tongue setting to hear a new word.

data.heading: Syllable beats
data.text: Tap once for each vowel beat: ami has two /a.mi/; ici has two /i.si/. Do not read every written consonant as an extra beat.

data.heading: Acute accent
data.text: é commonly marks /e/, as in été /ete/. Keep the tongue high and the sound steady.

data.heading: Grave and circumflex
data.text: è and ê often show open /ɛ/ in père /pɛʁ/ and fête /fɛt/. Lower the jaw slightly compared with /e/.

data.heading: Cedilla
data.text: ç means c is /s/ before a, o or u: garçon /ɡaʁsɔ̃/. A plain c before a often sounds /k/.

data.heading: Other marks
data.text: A diaeresis can signal separate vowels: Noël /nɔ.ɛl/. A grave accent on à distinguishes spelling from a, though both sound /a/.

data.heading: CH and J
data.text: ch in chat is /ʃ/; j in jour is voiced /ʒ/. Place fingers on your throat to feel voice vibration in /ʒ/.

data.heading: French R
data.text: The common /ʁ/ is produced near the back of the mouth. Practice rue /ʁy/ slowly; clarity matters more than forcing a harsh sound.

data.heading: Final letters
data.text: The t of chat and petit, and the s of vous, are silent in these isolated words. This is a pattern with exceptions, not a rule for every final letter.

data.heading: Spelling clusters
data.text: gn in montagne is /ɲ/. Split the word as /mɔ̃.taɲ/ and listen for the last consonant.

data.heading: What nasal means
data.text: For /ɔ̃/ in bon, air passes through nose and mouth during the vowel. Do not tack an English n onto the end.

data.heading: Three common targets
data.text: Compare bon /bɔ̃/, enfant /ɑ̃fɑ̃/ and pain /pɛ̃/. These are distinct targets in a broad metropolitan model.

data.heading: Regional variation
data.text: Un is often described as /œ̃/; many speakers merge it with /ɛ̃/. Recognize both realizations rather than treating one as wrong.

data.heading: Two more pairs
data.text: oi is /wa/ in moi; eu is /ø/ in deux. Read the pair as one target before saying the full word.

data.heading: Zero through three
data.text: Learn zéro /zeʁo/, un /œ̃/, deux /dø/, trois /tʁwa/. Count four objects with one beat per number.

data.heading: Four through six
data.text: Quatre /katʁ/, cinq /sɛ̃k/, six /sis/ in isolation. Cinq has a nasal vowel and a pronounced final /k/.

data.heading: Seven through ten
data.text: Sept /sɛt/, huit /ɥit/, neuf /nœf/, dix /dis/. Their isolated final consonants are audible.

data.heading: Retrieval
data.text: Cover the names; write 0–10 from memory. Then count backward from 10. Context can change the endings of six and dix; this drill uses isolated forms.

data.text: Build dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf. Dix is pronounced with /z/ before huit and neuf in these compounds.

data.heading: Twenty
data.text: Vingt is /vɛ̃/ in isolation. Connect the sound to the nasal vowel studied on day 6.

data.heading: Tens to sixty
data.text: Vingt 20, trente 30, quarante 40, cinquante 50, soixante 60. Learn tens as anchors before combining.

data.heading: Add units
data.text: For 22–29, join the ten and unit with a hyphen: vingt-deux, vingt-trois. Repeat for other decades.

data.heading: One after a ten
data.text: In the metropolitan pattern, 21, 31, 41, 51 and 61 use et un: vingt et un, trente et un.

data.heading: Seventy
data.text: 70 is soixante-dix (60 + 10); 71 is soixante et onze. Continue 72–79 with soixante + 12–19.

data.heading: Eighty
data.text: 80 is quatre-vingts (4 × 20). Its s drops before another number: 81 quatre-vingt-un.

data.heading: Ninety
data.text: 90 is quatre-vingt-dix (80 + 10); 99 is quatre-vingt-dix-neuf. 100 is cent.

data.heading: Variant awareness
data.text: Belgian and Swiss usage may use septante and nonante; the course teaches the metropolitan counting pattern first.

data.heading: Person
data.text: Je = I; tu = familiar singular you; il/elle = he/she. Nous = we; vous = formal or plural you; ils/elles = they.
data.example: je · tu · il/elle · nous · vous · ils/elles

data.heading: Être singular
data.text: The present forms change with person: je suis, tu es, il/elle/on est. Do not use a bare English-style verb form.
data.example: je suis · tu es · elle est

data.heading: Être plural
data.text: Nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont. In vous êtes, a linking /z/ is heard.
data.example: nous sommes · vous êtes · ils sont

data.heading: Meaning before complexity
data.text: Pair one pronoun with one verb form. Short combinations come before articles, adjective agreement and longer sentences.

data.heading: Sentence skeleton
data.text: Start with subject + conjugated verb + place: Je suis ici. The pronoun je and suis are a practiced pair.
data.example: Je suis ici. = I am here.

data.heading: Change the subject
data.text: Tu es ici. changes both pronoun and verb. Il est ici. uses the third-person form. Keep the place fixed while changing the pair.
data.example: Tu es ici. · Il est ici.

data.heading: Question by intonation
data.text: Tu es ici ? can be a yes/no question in conversation with rising intonation. The same written words can be a statement with falling intonation.
data.example: Tu es ici. ↗ Tu es ici ?

data.heading: First noun phrase
data.text: Un livre means a book; the article belongs with the noun. J’ai un livre adds a new verb; treat it as a model, not a full conjugation lesson yet.
